meta.title: Who really said "Insanity Is Hereditary. You Can Get It from Your Children"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Sam Levenson, credited by name in an Oklahoma paper on 6 April 1961. Ann Landers got it from a list of jokes a reader mailed her in 1978.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Insanity Is Hereditary. You Can Get It from Your Children'?
meta.ogDescription: “Landers’ Law” was not Landers’. The humorist Sam Levenson was being credited by name seventeen years earlier.

answer.label: Not Ann Landers — actually Sam Levenson
answer.authorDates: 1911–1980 · American humorist, teacher and television host
answer.sourceLine: The earliest printing Quote Investigator has found is 6 April 1961, in an Oklahoma newspaper column, and it already carries the credit: “Insanity is hereditary. You can get it from your children. —Sam Levenson.” Walter Winchell ran it the next day as “Sam Levenson’s merciless truth”, and Levenson put it in his own 1973 memoir. It reached Ann Landers’s column in 1978, in a reader’s list of comic “Laws”, where it was labelled “Landers’ Law” and signed with her name — which is where the modern credit comes from.

source.excerpt: “Insanity is hereditary. You can get it from your children. —Sam Levenson”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes: “the quip was ascribed to Sam Levenson by April 1961. He also included it in his 1973 memoir, and QI believes he probably crafted it.”

The earliest evidence QI located is 6 April 1961, in “Strayed From the Heard” by Connie Nelson in The Ada Weekly News of Ada, Oklahoma, page 4 — and Levenson is named right there in the item. One day later Walter Winchell’s syndicated column carried it as “Sam Levenson’s merciless truth”. Both citations are to subscription newspaper archives we could not open, so we are reporting them as QI’s findings.

Levenson used the line himself in In One Era and Out the Other (1973), page 21, where it is the announced subject of one of his talks. QI records verifying that page against scans of the Pocket Books edition. The book on the Internet Archive ↗ is lending-restricted, so we could not read the page either.

The Ann Landers link is documented rather than mysterious. On 26 March 1978 her column printed a batch of comic “Laws” a reader had sent in; alongside “Lippmann’s Law” sat “Landers’ Law: Insanity is hereditary — you can get it from your children. — Ann Landers.” QI reproduces the item ↗ and calls the self-ascription implausible.

The joke’s grey-hair twin ran the same course. The Rotarian of September 1967 ↗ carries it, per Quote Investigator, as a short poem on page 51 credited to Helen Gorn Sutin — “Our gray hair is hereditary: We get it from our kids!” — and a Dave Berg cartoon in Mad used it the following year.
source.excerptNote: As printed in the Ada, Oklahoma column of 6 April 1961, quoted by Quote Investigator. We have not read the newspaper page ourselves; it sits behind a subscription archive we cannot reach.
source.rightsNote: First printed in a newspaper in 1961 and reused by Levenson in a 1973 book, so this is comfortably inside copyright: everything published in the United States from 1931 onward remains protected. Treat it as in copyright — quote it with attribution rather than reusing it as free text. The attribution being wrong for decades does not put it in the public domain.

author.name: Sam Levenson
author.heading: About Sam Levenson
author.metaLine: 1911–1980 · American humorist, teacher and television host
author.bio: Samuel Levenson was an American humorist, writer, teacher, television host and journalist. He grew up in a large Jewish immigrant family in Brooklyn, graduated from Brooklyn College in 1934 and taught high-school Spanish for fifteen years before comedy became the job. From 1949 he was a fixture on CBS — a panellist on This Is Show Business, host of Two for the Money and of The Sam Levenson Show, and a guest on The Ed Sullivan Show twenty-one times. His material was almost entirely domestic: parents, children, relatives and the indignities of both. That is why this joke is so plausibly his, and why it travelled so well without him.

copyAttribution: "Insanity is hereditary. You can get it from your children." — Sam Levenson, credited by name in The Ada Weekly News (Ada, Oklahoma) on 6 April 1961 and by Walter Winchell the next day; Levenson used it again in his memoir In One Era and Out the Other (1973), p. 21. Not Ann Landers, whose column printed it in 1978 as "Landers’ Law" inside a reader-submitted list of comic maxims. In copyright.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This joke has been pinned on at least five well-known names. Quote Investigator’s article lists eight candidates in its opening line, which is usually a sign that a line escaped its author early.

items.why: Her column of 26 March 1978 printed it as “Landers’ Law” signed “Ann Landers” — but inside a list of mock adages a reader had mailed in, not as her own writing, and seventeen years after Levenson was being credited by name. QI ↗ calls the ascription implausible. Worth noting that “Ann Landers” was a pen name ↗: the column in 1978 was written by Esther “Eppie” Lederer.
Credited in print by 6 April 1961, endorsed by Walter Winchell the next day, and used by Levenson himself in his 1973 memoir. QI believes he probably crafted it ↗.

A Tucson newspaper column of 18 October 1968 offered it as “an old W. C. Fields goodie”. QI ↗ states plainly that it “has found no substantive support for this linkage” — and Fields had died in 1946 ↗, twenty-two years before that column ran.

items.scope: A columnist who declined the credit
items.why: Bombeck printed the line in January 1980 but explicitly did not claim it — she said she had seen it on a bumper sticker. Bombeck (1927–1996) ↗ is nevertheless one of the names it is most often given to. QI ↗

By March 1963 the pianist was using his own version — “Insanity is hereditary — we catch it from our children” — as reported by the columnist Herb Caen. QI ↗ notes it was already circulating by then. Levant (1906–1972) ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Sam Levenson made the joke; Ann Landers published somebody else’s list. Quote Investigator’s full account ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Sam Levenson was a Brooklyn schoolteacher who became one of American television’s most-watched humorists, and this is his register exactly: a one-line inversion of received wisdom, aimed squarely at parents. Heredity flows the wrong way, and the children are the affliction.

The line has had an unusually busy career. Between 1961 and 1981 it was credited to Levenson, borrowed by Oscar Levant, pinned on W. C. Fields, printed by Ann Landers under her own name, disclaimed by Erma Bombeck as bumper-sticker wisdom, and mutated into a joke about grey hair that Princess Grace of Monaco was using by 1981.
detailsBody: The 1978 Ann Landers item is the most instructive step in the chain, because it shows a misattribution being manufactured in public. The list of “Laws” was a reader’s joke format: attach a plausible name to each maxim. “Lippmann’s Law” went to Walter Lippmann, and “Landers’ Law” went to the columnist the reader was writing to. Printed in a syndicated column read by millions, a gag ascription became a citation.

The grey-hair variant is worth following for the same reason. It appeared as a credited poem in The Rotarian in September 1967, as a Dave Berg cartoon in Mad in October 1968, and as a remark by Princess Grace in People in November 1981 — three different media, three different names, one joke. Quote Investigator’s article tracks all of them.

Fields on 18 October 1968 with "no substantive support"; Ann Landers’s column of 26 March 1978 printed "Landers’ Law: Insanity is hereditary — you can get it from your children. — Ann Landers" within a reader-sent list of "Laws"; Erma Bombeck printed it in January 1980 saying she saw it on a bumper sticker; The Rotarian of September 1967 ran a grey-hair version credited to Helen Gorn Sutin; and People in November 1981 quoted Princess Grace using the grey-hair form.
Samuel Levenson (December 28, 1911 – August 27, 1980) was an American humorist, writer, teacher, television host and journalist.

"Ann Landers" was a pen name created by Chicago Sun-Times advice columnist Ruth Crowley in 1943 and taken over by Esther Pauline "Eppie" Lederer in 1955; the syndicated Ask Ann Landers column ran for 56 years.
Erma Louise Bombeck (February 21, 1927 – April 22, 1996) was an American humorist whose newspaper humor column on suburban home life was syndicated from 1965 to 1996.
Oscar Levant (December 27, 1906 – August 14, 1972) was an American concert pianist, composer, conductor and actor.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Sam Levenson’s In One Era and Out the Other; access is lending-restricted, so the page could not be read.
William Claude Dukenfield (January 29, 1880 – December 25, 1946), better known as W. C. Fields, was an American actor, comedian, juggler and writer.

Sam Levenson grew up in a large Jewish immigrant family in Brooklyn, New York, graduated from Brooklyn College in 1934, taught high school Spanish for fifteen years, was a panelist on CBS’s This Is Show Business from 1949 to 1954, hosted Two for the Money from 1956 and The Sam Levenson Show from 1959 to 1964, and appeared on Toast of the Town (The Ed Sullivan Show) twenty-one times.
